title: Weiss v. United States (1994)
summary: A commissioned military officer may be assigned to serve as a military judge without a second Appointments Clause appointment, and the lack of a fixed term for military judges does not violate due process.
notes:
Key line: Even assuming, arguendo, that the germaneness principle set forth in Shoemaker applies to the present situation, no second appointment is necessary because the role of military judge is germane to that of military officer. (Chief Justice Rehnquist)

Citation: 510 U.S. 163 (1994).

sections.Parties: The petitioners were two United States Marines, Weiss and Hernandez, each convicted at a court-martial after pleading guilty. The respondent was the United States. Weiss's case, No. 92-1482, was decided together with Hernandez's under the Court's Rule 12.2. Alan B. Morrison argued for the petitioners and Solicitor General Drew Days argued for the United States. The American Civil Liberties Union and the Air Force Appellate Defense Division filed amicus briefs supporting the Marines. The judges whose authority was challenged were military trial and appellate judges detailed to their duties by the Judge Advocates General of the services under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
sections.Material Facts: Weiss pleaded guilty at a special court-martial to one count of larceny under Article 121 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice and received three months of confinement, partial forfeiture of pay and a bad-conduct discharge. Hernandez pleaded guilty to possession, importation and distribution of cocaine and to conspiracy and was sentenced to twenty-five years of confinement, later reduced by the convening authority to twenty years, with forfeiture of pay, reduction in rank and a dishonorable discharge. Under Articles 26 and 66 of the Code, military trial judges and judges of the Courts of Military Review are commissioned officers who are members of a bar, detailed or assigned to judicial duty by the Judge Advocate General of their service. They serve no fixed term and may be returned to other duties. Every judge in petitioners' cases had already been commissioned as an officer through nomination by the President and confirmation by the Senate before being assigned to the bench.
sections.Procedural History: The Navy-Marine Corps Court of Military Review affirmed both convictions in separate appeals. The Court of Military Appeals granted plenary review in Weiss's case and, relying in part on its recent decision in United States v. Graf, rejected his arguments that military judges lacked authority because their appointments violated the Appointments Clause and that their lack of a fixed term violated the Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause, 36 M.J. 224. It then summarily affirmed Hernandez's conviction, 37 M.J. 252. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on November 3, 1993, and decided the cases on January 19, 1994, affirming both judgments. Chief Justice Rehnquist wrote for the Court.
sections.Issue: Two questions were presented. First, does the Appointments Clause of Article II, section 2, require a separate appointment before a commissioned officer, already appointed by the President with Senate consent, may act as a military trial or appellate judge, or does the current practice of detailing officers to judicial duty by the Judge Advocates General satisfy the Clause? Second, does the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment require that military judges have a fixed term of office in order to secure the independence and impartiality that a criminal defendant is entitled to expect from the judge who tries him?
sections.Holding: No second appointment is required. All the judges in these cases were commissioned officers already appointed under the Clause, and Congress did not create a separate office of military judge requiring a further appointment; the Code speaks of judges being detailed or assigned, in contrast to positions such as Chairman of the Joint Chiefs for which Congress expressly demanded a new appointment. Even if the germaneness principle of Shoemaker v. United States applies, judicial duties are germane to the duties of a military officer. The absence of a fixed term does not deny due process. Applying the deferential standard of Middendorf v. Henry rather than Mathews v. Eldridge, the Court found that history, in which military judges have never had tenure, and the Code's protections against command influence defeat the claim. Affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Rehnquist first rejected the argument that Buckley v. Valeo and its successors required a new appointment. Those cases mark the line between officers and employees; they say nothing about whether an officer already appointed needs another appointment when given new duties. The Code requires military judges to have qualifications such as bar membership, but special qualifications attach to many military assignments and do not signal a separate office. More telling, Congress used the words detailed and assigned for judges while expressly requiring Senate confirmation for top posts like the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, which shows it did not intend a second appointment for judges. The Court then assumed without deciding that Shoemaker requires new duties to be germane to the existing office and found the test met: nonjudicial officers convene courts-martial, refer charges and review sentences, so judging is not foreign to the military officer's role, and the military judge's position is less distinct from other military positions than a civilian judgeship is from other civilian offices. On due process, the Court explained that deference to Congress is at its apogee in military matters, so the question is whether the factors favoring fixed terms are so extraordinarily weighty as to overcome Congress's balance. Anglo-American military judges have never had tenure, Articles 26 and 37 shield judges from command influence and improper performance evaluation, and petitioners offered no evidence of actual partiality.

topics.lrs-s-germaneness: Military justice duties fell within the traditional responsibilities of commissioned officers.
topics.lrs-s-appointments-clause: Weiss asks whether assigning judicial duties to commissioned officers requires a second Appointments Clause appointment.

learning.separateOpinions: Unanimous in the judgment. Justice Souter concurred, reasoning that the Appointments Clause question should also ask whether military judges are principal or inferior officers, and concluding that they are inferior officers appointable in this way. Justice Ginsburg concurred briefly to stress that service members retain constitutional protections and that the Court's holding rests on the Code's safeguards. Justice Scalia, joined by Justice Thomas, concurred in part and in the judgment, joining Parts I and II-A but rejecting any balancing test for due process in favor of asking whether the challenged practice is rooted in the Nation's history.
